meta.title: Safety Orientation in Construction Environments
meta.description: Learn how to prepare for safe work, inspect the work area, select and use PPE, use tools safely, lift correctly, handle chemicals, respond to emergencies, and share safety responsibilities on construction sites.
meta.oshaStandard: 29 CFR 1926 Subparts C, D, E, F, G, I, J, K, L, M

lessons.safety-first-mental-preparation:
**Safety First and Mental Preparation**

Construction safety begins before the work starts. Workers must arrive at the jobsite mentally prepared — focused, alert, and free from conditions that could impair judgment or performance. Emotions such as anger or frustration, physical fatigue, personal distractions, medications, and impairment from substances can all interfere with the ability to recognize hazards and make safe decisions. Safety First means treating safe work as the highest priority on every task. No deadline or production pressure is more important than preventing injury. Workers should also recognize when a coworker's behavior signals that conditions are not right for safe work, and speak up or notify a supervisor before beginning.

• Safety First means making safe work the top priority on every task, every day.
• Anger, fatigue, impairment, and distractions are risk factors that increase injury likelihood.
• Workers must arrive mentally prepared before beginning any construction task.
• Recognizing when a coworker is unfit for safe work is also a safety responsibility.
lessons.work-area-inspection:
**Inspecting the Work Area**

Before beginning any task, workers should inspect the work area for hazards. A pre-task inspection looks for cluttered or blocked walkways, unguarded openings or edges, electrical hazards, fire hazards, stored materials that could shift or fall, and conditions that may have changed since the last shift. Good housekeeping is an ongoing duty — keeping walkways clear, removing debris, and organizing materials reduces slips, trips, falls, fires, and blocked emergency routes. Workers should correct hazards they can safely address and report conditions requiring supervisor or competent-person attention. Conditions that cannot be corrected must not be ignored.

• Inspect the work area for hazards before starting every task.
• Look for blocked walkways, electrical hazards, stored materials, and unguarded openings.
• Good housekeeping reduces slips, trips, falls, fires, and blocked emergency exits.
• Correct safe-to-fix hazards yourself; report all others to a supervisor immediately.
lessons.personal-protective-equipment:
**Personal Protective Equipment**

PPE protects workers from hazards that engineering and administrative controls have not eliminated. PPE must match the specific hazard — not all PPE protects against all hazards. Common construction PPE includes hard hats (overhead hazards), safety glasses and goggles (eye hazards), face shields (splashes and impacts), gloves (hand hazards), safety footwear (foot and puncture hazards), hearing protection (noise), respiratory protection (dust, fumes, vapors), high-visibility clothing (traffic and equipment exposure), and fall protection when working at height. All PPE must be inspected before each use and removed from service if damaged or worn.

• PPE must be matched to the specific hazard — different hazards require different protection.
• Hard hats protect against overhead hazards such as falling tools and materials.
• PPE does not eliminate hazards; it reduces the risk of injury from exposure.
• Inspect PPE before every use and replace damaged or worn equipment immediately.
lessons.tools-equipment-safe-practices:
**Safe Work Practices for Tools and Equipment**

Safe use of hand tools, power tools, electrical equipment, and machinery requires selection, inspection, and proper use before and during work. Workers must inspect tools and cords before use and remove damaged items from service rather than attempting field repairs. Damaged electrical cords must be taken out of use immediately. Machine guards must never be removed — they prevent contact with moving parts, pinch points, and flying debris. Power tools must be used only for their intended purpose. Workers must not operate any tool or piece of equipment they have not been trained to use. When equipment requires servicing, lockout/tagout procedures must be followed.

• Inspect all tools and cords before use; remove damaged items from service.
• Machine guards must never be removed regardless of production pressure.
• Damaged electrical cords must be taken out of service immediately.
• Never operate a tool or piece of equipment without proper training.
lessons.body-mechanics-lifting:
**Body Mechanics, Lifting, and Ergonomics**

Musculoskeletal injuries from lifting, carrying, pushing, and pulling are among the most common construction injuries. Safe lifting requires bending at the knees — not the waist — keeping the back straight, holding the load close to the body, and using leg strength to rise. Workers should not twist at the waist while carrying a load; instead, reposition the feet to change direction. Before lifting, assess the weight and get help or use a mechanical aid if the load is too heavy to lift alone. Position tools and materials at a comfortable working height when possible to reduce overhead reaching, sustained bending, and awkward postures.

• Bend at the knees, keep the back straight, and lift using leg strength.
• Keep the load close to the body and avoid twisting at the waist while carrying.
• Get help or use a mechanical aid for loads that are too heavy to lift alone.
• Position materials at a comfortable height to reduce awkward postures and reaching.
lessons.hazard-communication-chemicals:
**Hazard Communication and Chemical Emergencies**

Before using any hazardous chemical, workers must review the Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for that material. The SDS provides health hazard information, required PPE, first aid steps, and emergency response procedures. SDSs must be available at the jobsite and workers must know where they are kept. Workers should never attempt to identify a chemical by smelling or tasting it. If a chemical splashes into a worker's eyes or onto skin, flush the affected area with clean water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical attention. Workers must know the location of eyewash stations, safety showers, and emergency water sources before beginning any chemical work.

• Review the SDS before using any hazardous chemical on the jobsite.
• The SDS provides hazard information, required PPE, first aid, and emergency response.
• Never identify a chemical by smelling or tasting it.
• Chemical eye contact: flush with water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical attention.
lessons.fire-prevention-emergency:
**Fire Prevention and Emergency Response**

Construction sites present fire hazards from flammable materials, fuels, welding and cutting operations, electrical equipment, and debris accumulation. Workers should know the location of fire extinguishers, evacuation routes, and emergency assembly points before beginning work. A fire extinguisher may be used by a trained worker on a small, contained fire when the correct extinguisher type is available and a clear exit is behind them. When the fire is spreading, the worker is not trained, or the correct extinguisher is unavailable, the correct action is to evacuate immediately and call for emergency assistance. Workers must also know procedures for medical emergencies and understand site evacuation signals.

• Know the location of fire extinguishers, evacuation routes, and assembly points before work begins.
• Only attempt to fight a fire when it is small, you are trained, and you have the correct extinguisher.
• When the fire is spreading or you are not trained, evacuate and call for help.
• Understand site emergency signals and procedures for medical emergencies.
lessons.shared-safety-responsibilities:
**Shared Safety Responsibilities**

Construction site safety depends on employees, supervisors, and employers working together. Employees are responsible for following safety procedures, using required PPE, inspecting work areas, reporting hazards and near misses, and looking out for coworkers. Supervisors must enforce safe work practices, ensure crews have required training and equipment, and address unsafe conditions promptly. Employers are responsible for providing a safe worksite, complying with OSHA standards, training workers, maintaining required records, and correcting hazards. Reporting hazards and near misses is not troublemaking — it is one of the most effective ways workers help prevent future accidents and protect the entire crew.

• Safety is a shared responsibility among employees, supervisors, and employers.
• Employees must report hazards, near misses, and unsafe conditions promptly.
• Supervisors must enforce procedures and ensure workers have training and equipment.
• Reporting hazards and near misses helps prevent future injuries for the whole crew.

1.questionText: "Safety First" on a construction site means:

options.text: Getting the work done quickly before hazards are addressed
Leaving all safety decisions to the supervisor
Treating safe work as the highest priority on every task
Wearing PPE only when a supervisor is watching

2.questionText: Which of the following is most likely to put a worker and their coworkers at risk?

options.text: Taking time to inspect the work area
Communicating clearly with the crew
Working while angry, impaired, or fatigued
Following established safety procedures

3.questionText: The best time to inspect a work area for hazards is:

options.text: After completing the task
Only when an incident has occurred
Before beginning work on each task
At the end of the shift

4.questionText: True or False: Cluttered walkways, blocked exits, and poor housekeeping are not significant safety hazards on a construction site.

options.text: True
False

5.questionText: A damaged electrical cord is found on the jobsite. The safest course of action is to:

options.text: Tape the damaged section and continue use
Continue using it carefully until the end of the shift
Remove it from service or report it for replacement
Leave it in place and warn coworkers verbally

6.questionText: The reason PPE must be carefully matched to the task is that:

options.text: All types of PPE protect against all hazards equally
PPE is only required for new or untrained workers
PPE eliminates the hazard from the worksite
Different hazards require different types of protection

7.questionText: A worker drilling overhead into a ceiling surface should wear which of the following as minimum head protection?

options.text: Dust mask
Earplug
Hard hat
Face shield only

8.questionText: True or False: It is acceptable to temporarily remove a machine guard if it is slowing the pace of the job.

options.text: True
False

9.questionText: Which of the following describes the safest method for lifting a heavy object?

options.text: Bend at the waist, keep legs straight, and lift quickly
Hold the load far from the body to keep feet clear
Bend the knees, keep the back straight, and lift using leg strength
Twist at the waist while lifting to place the object to the side

10.questionText: Before working with a chemical on a construction site, the worker should:

options.text: Test it by smelling a small amount
Use it in the open air without any PPE
Assume it is safe if the container appears sealed
Review the Safety Data Sheet and follow all required precautions

11.questionText: A chemical splashes into a worker's face and eyes. The correct immediate response is to:

options.text: Cover the affected area and continue working
Rinse briefly with water and monitor for symptoms
Flush the affected area with water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical attention
Wait for a supervisor to evaluate the situation before taking action

12.questionText: A worker can safely attempt to extinguish a fire when:

options.text: The fire is spreading rapidly
They are untrained in fire extinguisher use
The fire is small, they are trained, and they have the correct type of extinguisher
All exits in the area have been blocked

13.questionText: Scrap materials and tools are piled in the middle of a pedestrian walkway. The correct response is to:

options.text: Step around the obstruction and keep working
Leave it for the housekeeping crew at end of day
Kick the debris aside and walk through
Move or report the hazard in accordance with site procedures

14.questionText: An employee is asked to operate a piece of equipment they have never used before. The correct first step is to:

options.text: Read the label and figure it out on the job
Watch a coworker operate it and then try independently
Use a familiar tool instead to avoid the problem
Ask a trained person or supervisor for instruction before beginning

15.questionText: True or False: Reporting hazards and near misses is primarily a way for supervisors to discipline employees.

options.text: True
False
